beats.intro: Lesson one. [[sub]]Introduction to ozone depletion: what the ozone layer is, how it gets damaged, and why that matters for the rest of this course.
beats.layers: Let's start with the sky above us. [[tropo]]The lowest part of the atmosphere is the troposphere. It's where we live and where weather happens, and it reaches about ten to fifteen kilometres up. [[strato]]Above it is the stratosphere, which climbs to about fifty kilometres. [[band]]Most of the stratosphere's ozone sits in one band, between about fifteen and thirty-five kilometres. That band is what we call the ozone layer. [[ninety]]Around ninety percent of all ozone is up here in the stratosphere. [[ten]]The other ten percent is down in the troposphere, close to us.
beats.molecule: So what is ozone? [[o2]]Ordinary oxygen, the kind we breathe, is two oxygen atoms bonded together: O two. [[split]]High in the stratosphere, ultraviolet light from the Sun is strong enough to split that pair into two single atoms. [[join]]A single atom soon joins another oxygen molecule, [[o3]]and makes a molecule of three oxygen atoms. That is ozone, O three. Sunlight keeps making it, all the time.
beats.sunscreen: And ozone does something vital in return. [[rays]]The Sun sends three kinds of ultraviolet light toward Earth. [[uvc]]U V C, the most dangerous, is stopped completely by the ozone layer. [[uvb]]U V B is mostly absorbed, but some gets through. [[uva]]U V A, the weakest, passes almost freely. [[shield]]That's why the ozone layer is often called our planet's sunscreen. [[harm]]Without it, more U V B would reach us: more skin cancer and cataracts, weaker immune systems, [[sea]]damage to plankton and the young fish that start the ocean's food chain, [[plastic]]and even plastics that crack and wear out sooner.
beats.ground: But ozone is not always a friend. [[same]]The ozone near the ground is exactly the same molecule, made a different way. [[cars]]Exhaust from cars and industry releases nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds. [[sun]]In sunlight, they react and form ozone right where we breathe. [[smog]]It's a main ingredient of smog, it irritates the lungs, and it's why cities issue air quality alerts on hot, sunny days. [[rule]]So remember: ozone high up protects us. Ozone down here harms us.
beats.q1: Quick check. Where is most of Earth's ozone?
beats.hole: In the nineteen seventies, scientists warned that certain industrial chemicals could damage the ozone layer. [[found]]In nineteen eighty-five, they found proof: a region of severely thinned ozone above Antarctica, [[grow]]and it came back every year, larger and deeper. [[du]]To measure ozone, scientists use Dobson units. Imagine squeezing all the ozone above one spot down to the ground: one Dobson unit is a layer just one hundredth of a millimetre thick. [[line]]Before nineteen seventy-nine, Antarctic readings never fell below two hundred and twenty Dobson units. [[def]]So any area below that line is called the ozone hole.
beats.poles: Why over the poles? [[vortex]]In the polar winter, strong winds circle the pole, a polar vortex, and lock the cold air in. [[clouds]]It gets so cold that thin clouds form in the stratosphere, polar stratospheric clouds. [[react]]On their icy surfaces, chlorine and bromine from industrial chemicals are turned into very reactive forms. [[spring]]When the Sun returns in late winter and early spring, they attack the ozone all at once, and the hole opens. [[arctic]]The Antarctic hole is the largest, but the Arctic has had serious losses too, notably in two thousand eleven and two thousand twenty.
beats.uses: Which chemicals? [[cfc]]The first identified were chlorofluorocarbons, or C F Cs. [[fridge]]They were everywhere: in fridges and air conditioners, [[foam]]in foam for insulation, mattresses and shoe soles, [[spray]]in aerosol sprays, medical inhalers, and fire extinguishers, [[farm]]and related substances were used as fumigants in agriculture. [[stable]]Down here, C F Cs are very stable and harmless. That's exactly the problem: [[drift]]they last long enough to drift up into the stratosphere.
beats.chain: Up there, the story changes. [[hit]]Strong ultraviolet light hits a C F C molecule and breaks off a chlorine atom. [[attack]]The chlorine grabs one oxygen atom from an ozone molecule, [[left]]leaving ordinary oxygen behind. [[free]]Then that pair meets a loose oxygen atom, the oxygen atoms pair up, and the chlorine is set free again, [[again]]ready to destroy the next ozone molecule. [[count]]Because it is never used up, a single chlorine atom can destroy up to one hundred thousand ozone molecules before it is finally removed.
beats.cure: Could we simply put ozone back? [[ship]]Ideas like shipping ozone up into the stratosphere were studied, [[no]]but ozone is too unstable, and it would be far too costly and impractical. [[only]]The only real cure is to stop producing and using ozone-depleting substances. [[law]]And that takes countries acting together: the international law you'll meet in Lessons two and three.
beats.q2: Quick check. Why can one chlorine atom destroy so much ozone?
beats.climate: Last, ozone depletion and climate change. [[two]]They are two different problems, handled by two separate sets of treaties. [[linked]]But they are linked. [[ghg]]Many ozone-depleting substances are also powerful greenhouse gases. A kilogram of C F C eleven warms the planet more than four and a half thousand times as much as a kilogram of carbon dioxide; C F C twelve, more than ten thousand times. [[bonus]]So phasing them out has also slowed climate change. [[cool]]In the other direction, a warmer world wants more cooling, which puts pressure on the refrigerants the ozone treaty controls. [[cold]]And changing weather patterns can bring the cold conditions that destroy ozone more often, as over the Arctic in two thousand twenty.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Most ozone sits in the stratosphere, where it screens out harmful ultraviolet light. Ozone near the ground is a pollutant. [[w2]]Chemicals like C F Cs release chlorine and bromine high up, and one atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. [[w3]]Cold and the polar vortex make the damage worst over the poles, which is the ozone hole. [[w4]]Ozone depletion and climate change are different problems, but closely linked. [[end]]Now, a short practice.
